title: Equality, truthiness, null and undefined
objectives: Predict `===`, `==` and `Object.is` results using the few coercion rules worth knowing, and test for `NaN` correctly
Recite the falsy values and fix truthiness bugs: `{count && …}` rendering `0`, an empty array being truthy, `filter(Boolean)` dropping zeros
Explain that objects and arrays compare by identity, and compare by an id or specific fields instead
Model absence in TypeScript — `?:` vs `| undefined` vs `| null` under `strictNullChecks` — and predict what JSON does to each

sources.title: TypeScript Handbook: Everyday Types (null and undefined)
TypeScript 5.5 release notes: inferred type predicates

questions.explanation: Loose equality has a special rule: `null` and `undefined` equal each other and nothing else — which is why `x == null` is a common one-step "null or undefined" check, and why `null == 0` is false. Strict equality never converts, and `null` and `undefined` are different types. `NaN` is unequal to everything, itself included, under both `==` and `===`.

questions.prompt: Which of these values make `if (value) { … }` run its body? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The falsy list is short: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN` (plus `document.all`). Everything else is truthy — any non-empty string, including `"0"` and `"false"`, and every object, including an empty array. That's why a query-string flag of `"false"` passes an `if`, and `if (!results)` never catches an empty result list.

questions.prompt: `{unread && <Badge count={unread} />}` shows a stray `0` in the header when there are no unread messages. Why?

options.text: `&&` returns its left side when that side is falsy, so the expression is `0` — and React renders numbers
React renders every falsy value as text; `false` would show up too
`Badge` renders its `count` prop even when it is `0`

questions.explanation: `a && b` evaluates to `a` when `a` is falsy — here the number `0`, which React renders as text. React renders nothing for `false`, `null` and `undefined` (it treats them as holes), which is why the bug only appears for numbers. Badge never renders at all. Fix the condition, not the component: `unread > 0 && …`.

questions.prompt: `selected.includes({ id: 3 })` is `false`, though `selected` holds an item with `id: 3`. What's the right fix?

options.text: `selected.some((s) => s.id === 3)` — objects compare by identity, so compare the id

questions.explanation: Every equality check — `===`, SameValueZero in `includes`, `Object.is` — compares objects by identity, and the literal `{ id: 3 }` is a new object, so no search by value can find it. `indexOf` fails the same way (and `includes` doesn't use `==`). The JSON trick happens to work on this exact item but breaks on key order or extra fields. Decide what makes two items the same (the `id`) and compare that.

questions.prompt: For which pairs do `Object.is(a, b)` and `a === b` give **different** answers? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `Object.is` is `===` with two fixes: `NaN` equals itself, and `0` and `-0` are different. Neither converts types, so `"1"` vs `1` and `null` vs `undefined` are `false` under both, and two object literals are different objects under every equality check. React uses `Object.is` to compare state and effect dependencies.

questions.prompt: To clear a user's nickname you send `PATCH /users/1` with `body: JSON.stringify({ nickname: undefined })`. What does the server receive?

options.text: `{}` — JSON drops properties whose value is `undefined`, so it looks like "change nothing"

questions.explanation: `undefined` isn't a JSON value. In an object, `JSON.stringify` omits the property; in an array it writes `null`. So the server sees no `nickname` key at all and changes nothing. `null` is the JSON way to say "explicitly empty" — send `{ nickname: null }` to clear. (`undefined` can never appear in JSON text, so the third option isn't valid JSON.)

questions.prompt: In a project with `strict: true` (the default since TS 6.0), what does TypeScript do with `function initial(u: { middle?: string }) { return u.middle[0]; }`?

options.text: It compiles, and returns `undefined` when `middle` is missing
It compiles; you only find out at runtime, when `middle` is missing
It's only an error with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` enabled

questions.explanation: `strict` includes `strictNullChecks`, under which reading an optional property gives `string | undefined`, and indexing a possibly-undefined value is an error until you check it (`u.middle?.[0]`, or an `if`). With `strictNullChecks` off — the default before TS 6.0 unless `strict` was set — it compiles and throws at runtime. `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is a separate flag about whether `?:` accepts an explicit `undefined`.

prompts.prompt: Return early when `value` is `null` **or** `undefined`, in a single comparison — and only then (keep `0` and `""`).
prompts.explanation: Loose equality's special case: `null` and `undefined` equal each other and nothing else, so `value == null` is true for exactly those two values. `=== null` would miss `undefined`; `!value` would also catch `0`, `""` and `false`.

prompts.prompt: Reject a price that failed to parse (`Number("abc")` is `NaN`).
prompts.code: if (Number.___(price)) throw new Error("price is not a number");
prompts.explanation: `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself, so `price === NaN` is always `false`. `Number.isNaN` checks for the actual `NaN` value; the global `isNaN` converts its argument first (`isNaN("abc")` is `true`).

prompts.prompt: Render the badge only when there are unread messages — and never render a stray `0`.
prompts.explanation: Make the left side of `&&` a boolean. `unread && …` evaluates to `0` when there are none, and React renders numbers; `unread > 0` is `false`, which React skips.

prompts.prompt: Is `item` already in `selected`? Both hold separately fetched objects.
prompts.explanation: `includes(item)` compares identity, and a refetched object is a different object. `some` with a predicate lets you say what "the same item" means — the same `id`.

prompts.prompt: Type a field the API always sends, using `null` when there is no value.
prompts.code: type User = { id: string; deletedAt: string ___ };
prompts.explanation: `| null` describes a key that is always present but may hold `null` — the shape of a nullable database column. `deletedAt?: string` would describe a key that may be missing, which is not what the API sends, and would make a check against `null` look unnecessary.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: Two array literals are two objects, so `===` is `false`. `==` converts an object compared with a primitive into a primitive first: `[1, 2]` becomes `"1,2"`, which matches. For `[] == false`, the boolean becomes `0`, `[]` becomes `""`, `""` becomes `0`, and `0 == 0`. Reasoning like this is why the rule is `===`.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `filter(Boolean)` keeps truthy values, and `0` is falsy, so a real score of zero disappears along with `null` and `undefined`. Filter on what you mean — `scores.filter((s) => s != null)` gives `[0, 7, 3]` (and, since TS 5.5, is typed `number[]`).

snippets.code: console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: null, c: [undefined, 1] }));
snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `undefined` isn't a JSON value. As an object property it's omitted (`a` is gone); inside an array it becomes `null`, so the other elements keep their positions. `null` is valid JSON and is kept. That asymmetry is why `null` is the way to say "explicitly empty" over the wire.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `includes` uses SameValueZero, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself and `-0` as equal to `0`. `indexOf` uses strict equality, under which `NaN` equals nothing, so it can never be found and you get `-1`. Same array, same value, two answers.
